title: Jonah
summary: Jonah is a biblical book focused on prophetic resistance, Gentile repentance, and divine mercy.
historical_context: Jonah exposes the prophet's resistance while highlighting God's mercy toward Nineveh.
ancient_near_east_context: Jonah belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Jonah should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Jonah as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Minor Prophets, book 5 of 12, Jonah contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting prophetic resistance, Gentile repentance, and divine mercy to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Jonah as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Jonah uses narrative within Minor Prophets, book 5 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Jonah helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars recognize collection and editorial shaping
date_ranges: 8th-5th centuries BCE, depending on the prophet
Final forms often reflect later collection and editing
original_audience: Israel and Judah under covenant accountability before and after exile
historical_setting: Assyrian, Babylonian, and post-exilic settings across the prophetic corpus
canonical_role: Jonah anchors prophetic resistance, Gentile repentance, and divine mercy within Minor Prophets, book 5 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read prophetic poetry, irony, and symbolic action

related_objects.notes: Nineveh is the destination and testing ground of Jonah's mission.
Nineveh's repentance is central to the narrative.
The book confronts Jonah with God's mercy toward outsiders.
Jonah is framed through prophetic calling and resistance.
Assyria gives the mission its political and emotional weight.
